en: Compiled by the Sramana Wonhyo of海东 (Haidong).
Below this, the non-awakening (*abodha*) is elucidated. This section contains two parts: first, the fundamental non-awakening;
second, from "Furthermore" (*fùcì*) onwards, the derivative non-awakening. Within the first part, two points are established: first, the actual elucidation of the basis of non-awakening.
The first establishes original enlightenment (benjue). The second clarifies that original enlightenment exists in dependence upon non-enlightenment (bujue).
The statement that "because one does not know the single reality of *tathatā* as it truly is, the mind of non-enlightenment arises" refers precisely to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
This is like being disoriented regarding directions;
that which possesses such a thought is the movement of thought within the marks of karma and so forth.
This is like a false direction.
Just as there is no separate "oblique direction" apart from the cardinal directions,
the oblique direction is itself the cardinal direction.
Therefore, it is said that mindfulness has no self-characteristic and is not separate from original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*).
Next, the meaning of original enlightenment in relation to non-enlightenment (*a-prabodha*) is clarified.
What is called "non-enlightenment" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).
The deluded mind is the mind that, failing to realize its own arising, grasps at various signs;
this refers to the root while taking up the branches.
One who can know names and meanings is called a "True Awakened One," because through the deluded mind one comes to know names and meanings.
When there is speech that speaks of true awakening,
this is called the discourse capable of expressing true awakening.
It must rely on the delusive thoughts arising from non-awakening (*abodha*).

To say that if one were separated from non-awakening, there would be no self-characteristic of true awakening (*tathatā*) that could be described, clarifies that the true awakening being discussed necessarily depends upon non-awakening.
If they do not depend on one another,
they lack their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa); even if they exist by depending on others, they still lack their own specific characteristics.
Since intrinsic characteristics do not exist, how could there be extrinsic characteristics?
This demonstrates that all phenomena are unapprehendable.
As stated in the following passage:
one should know that all defiled phenomena [are as follows].
Pure dharmas all exist in mutual dependence;
they have no self-characteristics that can be described.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If, in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there were even as much as a hair’s breadth of reality,
then ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) would also have to be real."
This is what is meant.
Furthermore, below this, the second section clarifies the lack of awareness regarding the branches and their sub-branches.
Within this, there are first the three characteristics.
This subtle [aspect] still resides in the state of the ālayavijñāna;
the latter six coarse aspects are the remaining seven consciousnesses.
However, looking toward that fundamental ignorance,
all [states] that have arisen from it are collectively termed "branch-and-tip non-awakening."
Regarding the phrase "the karmic characteristic of ignorance": it refers to the karmic characteristic produced by ignorance.
It has the meaning of "arising and moving," which is the meaning of "karma" (action).
Therefore, it is said that the movement of the mind is called the "characteristic of karma.
The phrase "awakening is non-movement" is an inverse explanation;
it refers to the time when one attains initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).
It is eternally unmoving;
one should know that present movement arises solely from non-awakening.
That which is subject to movement entails suffering; for instance, when one attains tranquility, that tranquility is bliss.
Therefore, it is now said that movement itself is suffering.
If the fruit does not depart from the cause, then ignorance is the absence of origination,
and the characteristic of karma is the absence of suffering. Thus,
there is neither suffering nor origination.
They exist simultaneously and are not separate from one another; yet,
although the characteristic of karma undergoes arising and ceasing, [the underlying nature remains].
It is most subtle, where subject and object are not yet differentiated;
ignorance is likewise so.
As stated in the *Asaṃjñika-śāstra*:
"Question: What are the characteristics and what is the object of this consciousness?
Answer: Its characteristics and its object cannot be distinguished."
They are of one essence and without difference.
Question: If this is so, how is it known that they exist?
Answer: By way of their functional activity.
One knows that this consciousness is capable of producing all matters of afflictions, karma, and retribution,
just as ignorance constantly arises.
Can this ignorance be conceptually differentiated?
If it can be conceptually differentiated,
it is not called ignorance; if it cannot be conceptually differentiated, [it is called ignorance].
The correspondence does not exist;
yet it exists as both existence and non-existence,
and this is also due to matters such as desire and hatred.
Just as one knows that there is ignorance,
so it is with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This is stated in the *Abhidharmapiṭaka-sūtra*.
The same applies to these and other such passages;
they specifically concern the characteristics of karma.
Thus it is said.
The second, the aspect of seeing, is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The third is the aspect of the objective realm (*ālambana-nimitta*).
This is the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the *ālayavijñāna*.
As it is said in the four-fascicle sutra:
"For example, like the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)."
One suddenly discriminates one's own mind as manifesting the body, the establishment of the body, the requisites, and so forth.
Regarding "suddenly discriminating":
This is the characteristic of the perceiver;
one's own mind, as well as what appears before it and so forth,
is the characteristic of the perceived object.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states this in the same way.
Such passages as these [are to be cited].
These two are explained in reference to the latter two characteristics;
although they possess two parts, [they are so designated].
It does not depart from the characteristic of karma;
this is the gateway of "representation-only" (vijñaptimātra).
Although the characteristic of karma lacks both subject and object, it is nonetheless established as such.
It contains two parts;
it consists of only these two.
These three are all subsumed within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
However, from the perspective of being deluded by karma and afflictions,
there is no distinction between the characteristics of karma, such as its movement, transformation, and differentiation.
Therefore, it is said in summary:
it is the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna),
and it is the wind of ignorance (avidyā-vāyu).
Regarding the aspect of the meaning of movement,
there are distinctions in the shifting and turning from the subtle to the coarse.
Therefore, they are subdivided and established as three types of characteristics.
Furthermore, these three—
However, because it is moved by ignorance, it resides in the eighth [consciousness];
whereas the latter six are moved by objective spheres, they reside in the seven consciousnesses.
It is precisely for this reason that—
It is said that the seven consciousnesses arise and perish exclusively;
they do not share the two meanings possessed by the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding the statement that the six characteristics arise because there are objective conditions (*ālambana*): this refers to the aforementioned subtle characteristics.
Based on the ability to see, the present object-field appears;
the object-field does not move the ability to see.
These are the latter six characteristics.
It is moved by the objective spheres manifested by those [six consciousnesses];
it is not these six that can manifest those objects.
Such is the distinct meaning.
Speaking in general terms:
it is said that the former also still relies upon its own manifested object,
while the latter can in turn serve as the supporting object for the former.
Now, within this treatise, it is appropriate to proceed by way of a specific topical division; therefore,
it is said that because there is an object, six kinds of characteristics arise.
As stated in the original sutra:
"Blown and stirred by the winds of objective realms,
the waves of the seven consciousnesses roll on."
This refers precisely to that.
Among the six characteristics,
it is the first characteristic.
This is the seventh consciousness.
Next are the four characteristics;
these are the four aggregates of the evolving consciousness.
The latter characteristic is the retributive fruit produced with the aggregate of formations as its cause.
Regarding the characteristic of "speech and wisdom":
this seventh consciousness is the beginning of the coarse [level of mind].
It is called the beginning because it is associated with discernment (*prajñā*) as it discriminates between "self" and "what belongs to the self."
It is called the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). As stated in the *Bhāryāsūtra*:
"Regarding these six consciousnesses, it is the wisdom of the mental factors (*citta-dharma*)."
It does not abide for even a single moment.
That which is called "wisdom among mental factors" is the mental factor of discernment (*prajñā*).
Therefore, it is known that the characteristic of wisdom herein resides precisely in the seventh consciousness.
Regarding the statement that "the mind arises based on objects": this refers to the arising of the seventh consciousness based on the characteristics of the aforementioned objects.
This occurs when one is in the wholesome realms.
Discriminating attractive phenomena as "I" and "mine," while dwelling in the evil realms.
One discriminates unloved phenomena as "I" and "mine";
therefore, it is said that one discriminates between the loved and the unloved. To speak fully:
One conceives the perceiving faculty as the self and the perceived objects that appear before it as "mine";
now, however, the explanation proceeds directly from the perspective of what is manifested by these marks.
Therefore, it is said that [the seventh consciousness] depends solely upon its object.

Furthermore, although this seventh consciousness universally takes as its objects both the *ālaya*— which is the capacity for seeing— and the appearance of the object, [it is still said to depend on the object].
However, this objective realm does not exist apart from the perceiving subject,
just as a reflection in a mirror does not exist apart from the mirror's surface.
This seventh consciousness simply turns inward and conceives of itself as "I" and "mine."
This is because it is not reckoned as being external.
In other passages, it is said that [the mind] takes the ālayavijñāna as its object,
but it is not said that it takes external objects as its object.
Furthermore, because it is explained in brief,
it refers specifically to the objects of the grasping at a self; therefore, it is said that consciousness takes them as its conditions.
Because it eliminates the objects of grasping at a self, it is not said that it also takes an objective sphere as its condition.
Question: How is this known?
This seventh consciousness not only takes the mind as its object,
but also takes objective realms as its object.
There are two proofs for this.
First, based on the principle of inference (anumāna);
second, based on authoritative testimony (āptāgama).
Regarding the principle of inference:
This mind-faculty necessarily shares the same object of perception as the mental consciousness.
"This is the proposition (*pakṣa*).
Because it serves as the uncommon support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*) for that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
this is the statement of the reason (*hetu*)."
All those that serve as uncommon bases necessarily share the same object as their supported [mental states],
just like the eye faculty and so forth.
This refers to the statement "conforming to the same category.
Alternatively, that which has different objects of cognition must not be a non-common basis.
The phrase "the mental faculty and so forth are extinguished in succession" is a statement of exclusion (*pariyāya*).
In this manner, there are infinite [applications of] thesis, reason, and example.
Therefore, it is known that the mental faculty (manas) also takes the six objects as its conditions.
If one were to say that this mental faculty and the mental consciousness do not share the same object, [it would be incorrect].
Furthermore, the eye and the visual consciousness need not necessarily share the same object,
because both are uncommon supports (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*). This is the case for the sense-faculties that serve as the bases for the visual consciousness and so forth.
Since that is not the case, because there is no similar class [of entity],
the argument cannot be established.
If one says that this mind is not the non-common support,
then there would be no non-common support,
and consciousness should not arise.
This is merely the fault of contradicting one's own teachings,
as it is stated in the Buddha’s sūtras.
Because the eye is unimpaired, visual consciousness arises;
and so on, up to: because the mind is unimpaired.
"Consciousness arises," and so forth,
as explained at length. Furthermore,
the treatise states that this is its unique support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*).
Therefore, it is known that this intention takes only consciousness as its object and does not take other objects;
thus, this argument is not established.
If one relies on this,
the dependent mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its object.
It should be known that the mental faculty (*manas*), which serves as the basis,
likewise faces all phenomena (*dharma*).
Therefore, this mental consciousness also takes its own substance as an object,
because it possesses a self-verifying portion (svasaṃvedanabhāga);
it also takes as objects the mental factors (caitasika-dharma) that are associated with itself.
Because there is no dharma capable of obstructing it,
those mental factors turn away from realizing their own intrinsic nature.
There is a self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga); therefore, it does not transcend [the object],
as both share the same focal object (ālambana).
It should be known that this principle applies to all eight consciousnesses.
This is how it is understood.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
"The explanation of seeking defilement and purity has already been given.
The verse from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
The grasper and the grasped—
these two are merely the radiance of mind.
So too are the radiance of greed and the radiance of faith.
"The two lights are the non-dual dharma.
The commentary states:
Regarding the first half [of the verse]:
Those who establish Consciousness-Only should know that there is the grasper and the grasped.
It is solely the light of mind.
The latter half refers to the light of afflictions such as greed.
The light of wholesome dharmas such as faith—
these two lights likewise possess neither the dharma of defilement nor the dharma of purity.
Because there are no phenomena such as desire or faith that exist separately from the light of the mind;
this passage serves as proof.
Therefore, it is known.
All mental factors (caitta-dharma) are likewise illumined by the light of the mind; therefore,
they are not separate from the light of the mind.
Because it is not separate from the light of the mind,
it is itself the light of the mind.
It is like an image in a mirror, which is illuminated by the light of the mirror.
Therefore, this image does not depart from the light of the mirror;
because it does not depart,
it is itself the light of the mirror.
One should know that the principle herein is likewise;
for although it resembles a reflected image, [it is not so].
There is no separate fundamental dharma that is not an object of perception;
for if there were a fundamental dharma whose mental factors were distinct from the mental factors of the reflected image,
then the principle of having a single common object of perception would not be established.
Regarding authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*),
as the Ten-Scroll Sūtra states:
"Those seven kinds of consciousness..."
It arises based on the mindfulness and contemplation of various objects.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The wind of objects blows and stirs [it]."
"The seven consciousnesses arise as waves.
Now, within this treatise,
the meaning of that sūtra is explained as follows:
Because there are objective conditions (*ālambana*),
six kinds of aspects (*nimitta*) further arise;
this is known from such passages as these.
Next, as for the second characteristic, that of continuity, it is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
It is coarse discrimination.
Pervadingly taking all things as its object and attaining a long-lasting continuity is called the characteristic of continuity.
Furthermore, this consciousness gives rise to craving,
which draws forth and sustains past karmas and also moistens rebirth.
Because it causes the continuity of future karmic retribution,
it is called "continuous consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "relying on wisdom," it means relying on the characteristics of the preceding wisdom.
This refers to the initial arising of the continuum.
Its basis is subtle, consisting solely of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Because that which can depend [upon it] is coarse and fully gives rise to suffering and pleasure,
it is said that "suffering and pleasure arise. Furthermore, this refers to the characteristic of the wisdom that serves as the basis.
Abiding with internal conditions,
this continuous consciousness resembles the eye.
Because it runs everywhere toward external objects,
just like cognition;
thus it is said that "cognition arises as thought."
The arising of a thought is itself the conceptualization of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-vikalpa*).
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is associated with this coarse attachment,
for it ranges everywhere across all objects.
Because verbal expression is uninterrupted,
next is the characteristic of grasping, which is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Next is the characteristic of calculating names, which is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Next is the section on the characteristics of the arising of karma; this is the text concerning the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
It is self-evident and does not require an elaborate explanation.
Furthermore, from "next" onwards:
Third, the clarification of similarities and differences.

Regarding the statement that "the untainted ignorance is the nature of differentiation within the delusive manifestation following defilement, and it is the differentiation within the delusive manifestation of defilement": the untainted [ignorance] is the differentiation within the delusive manifestation following defilement.
Ignorance is the fundamental defilement of illusion;
what is it? That ignorance—
This contradicts the nature of equality;
therefore, the nature of all defiled phenomena that arise from it is inherently differentiated.
The untainted dharmas accord with the nature of equality;
they simply abide in their own nature.
There should be no distinction;
however, because it follows the distinctions among defiled phenomena,
one speaks of distinctions within the untainted (anāsrava).
Why is this? Because there are distinctions in the defiled illusory manifestations corresponding to that karmic consciousness,
there are likewise distinctions in the untainted virtuous qualities of original enlightenment.
Furthermore, in order to counteract those various forms of defilement,
the distinctions of the myriad virtues of awakened awareness are established;
therefore, it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
There are distinctions only in accordance with those defilements;
there is no distinction by way of intrinsic nature.
However, this defilement and purity are entirely mutually dependent;
in their nature, they do not exist as anything at all.
Therefore, it is called an illusion.
The preceding section, which extensively elaborated upon the "Establishment of the Thesis" (*siddhānta*) regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind,
is now complete.
Furthermore, from "Below this" onwards is the second section, which extensively explains the causes of arising and ceasing. Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the meaning of arising and ceasing based on the principle of dependent origination.
Regarding the second point, "the consciousnesses arising from the perfuming of ignorance," the following section further elucidates the essential nature and characteristics of the causal basis;
first, it provides a general presentation.

The subsequent detailed explanation states that as for "causes and conditions," it refers to the essence of the *ālaya*-consciousness itself undergoing transformation to give rise to the birth and cessation of all phenomena.
This is the cause of arising and ceasing.
All phenomena that arise and cease support one another through their subtle and coarse characteristics.
And it arises.
This is the condition for arising and ceasing,
as the sutra says:
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome,
furthermore, the ground of the abiding of ignorance (avidyāvāsabhūmi) perfumes the essence of the mind, causing it to transform into the various consciousnesses.
It is called the cause of arising and ceasing;
the various consciousnesses that arise are the mutual supporting causes and conditions for their transformation.
As stated in the text below:
"All causes of defilement are termed ignorance."
Therefore, in this present passage,
both meanings are present.
When it says that sentient beings depend upon the mind, it refers to all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
They arise through aggregation;
therefore they are called "sentient beings," yet they lack intrinsic nature.
Because it relies solely upon the substance of the mind (*citta*),

it is said that "relying on the mind" refers to the dependent sentient beings, which are merely the mental faculty (*manas*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); thus, it is said that the mental faculty and mental consciousness revolve.
This indicates the two topical headings.
Regarding the meaning of this: the following section explains these two topical headings.
The preliminary explanation of "intention" (āśaya) has three parts:
first, a brief clarification of intention;
second, an extensive analysis of intention.
Therefore, from here on, the conclusion is established as "mind-only.
First, regarding the phrase "relying upon the ālayavijñāna":
The preceding explanation of the meaning of "relying on the mind" has been concluded.
Its characteristic is fundamental ignorance,
which directly relies upon the substance of consciousness.
Because it exists,
it is said that ignorance exists in dependence upon consciousness,
as stated in the preceding passage.
This consciousness has two meanings:
first, the meaning of awakening;
second, the meaning of non-awakening.
This refers precisely to this.
The four-fascicle sutra says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha."
Perfumed by beginningless false and evil habits,
it is called the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
the ground where ignorance dwells.
It should be known that the ground of abiding ignorance coexists with the seven consciousnesses.
It is not subsumed within the seven consciousnesses, nor is it the seed that is perfumed by them.
Regarding the statement "arising through non-awakening," the substance of the mind is perfumed by this ignorance.
It is called "arising" because of the production and cessation of its activities;
furthermore, it is this very essence of mind.
Due to the permeation of ignorance,
it transforms into that which is capable of seeing,
and so on, until it transforms into [the state of]...
The continuity of arising thoughts:
such is the substance of the mind,
which possesses these five functions.
Because it gives rise to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) with respect to objects,
it is called "mind" (*manas*).
This is the fifth [consciousness] herein.
It is still this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
yet by way of its meaning as that which arises subsequently,
it is generally included within the category of the mind (*manas*).
From "this intention" onwards is the second part,
the detailed explanation,
which opens up the five aforementioned functions.
The designation of the five consciousnesses and the meaning of the initial karma-consciousness have already been explained as before.
As for what are called the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna), they possess the characteristic of being able to perceive;
they evolve by taking objects as their conditions,
and are thus named evolving consciousnesses.
However, there are two aspects to the evolving consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna):
if one speaks of ignorance (avidyā),
it is that which is moved and that which is able to see.
That which is called "transforming consciousness" exists within the ālayavijñāna according to its respective objects.
That which is moved and capable of seeing is called the evolving consciousness;
this refers to the seven consciousnesses.
The two meanings are distinct and must not be conflated.
Furthermore, there is a passage that states:
All those that are capable of seeing are collectively termed *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses),
which thus encompass all eight consciousnesses.
Now, the "transforming characteristic" (pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa) herein refers to the first of the three meanings [of the dependent nature].
As for the "manifesting characteristic" (pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa), it is precisely the "object-aspect" (viṣaya-lakṣaṇa) among the aforementioned three characteristics.
However, herein, in order to clarify that there are no distinct objective images apart from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*),
the manifesting subject is cited to illustrate the manifested object.
Regarding the statement, "just as a bright mirror manifests forms and appearances," the four-fascicle *Sūtra* says:
"O Mahāmati, it is extensively taught that there are three kinds of consciousness."
The eight characteristics are explained in detail. What are the three?
They are the true consciousness, the manifesting consciousness, and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena.
Just as a bright mirror holds all forms and images,
so too does the locus of the manifesting consciousness appear.
Furthermore, in this passage,
the meaning of "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) is explained as follows: "At all times."
It arises spontaneously;
because it is always present before one,
you should know this.
The manifesting consciousness definitely resides in the eighth [consciousness];
its karmic consciousnesses and so forth serve as its basis.
Its characteristics are exceedingly subtle;
how can one forcibly place it within the seven consciousnesses?
Is this not quite extraordinary?
Regarding the statement that it manifests immediately upon encountering the five sense objects:
whatever signs arise do not depart from seeing, for they manifest solely within the mirror of the seer.
It is said that it appears immediately upon being confronted;
yet, speaking in terms of ultimate reality,
it also manifests as a dharma-object (dharmāyatana).
Furthermore, this has been illustrated by way of coarse objects; it is merely a brief enumeration.
Question: What is the breadth or narrowness of the objective sphere of this consciousness?
In this treatise,
only the five sense objects are discussed.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
The ālayavijñāna discerns and manifests the objective realm, one's own body, the means of subsistence,
and the vessel-world simultaneously, rather than sequentially.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"This [consciousness] evolves by means of discerning two kinds of objects:
first, by discerning internal appropriation (*ādāna*)."
It refers to the discernment of the thoroughly imagined nature,
the habitual tendencies of false attachment,
and the various material sense faculties.
The basis upon which the faculties rely refers to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
There is only the discernment of the habitual tendencies of false attachment.
Second, the discernment of the external, partless, and characteristic environment refers to the discernment of the basis.
Because it takes the internal appropriated *ālaya-vijñāna* as its object-condition,
it exists at all times without interruption.
The characteristics of the vessel-world are like the flame of a lamp at the moment it arises.
The internal appropriating consciousness externally emits light;
such is the ālaya-vijñāna.
The principle of origination regarding the internal objective sphere of appropriated objects and the external objective sphere of the receptacle world.
It should be known that it is likewise so.
As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:
The objects apprehended by this consciousness are of four kinds,
namely: those comprised of sense-fields, sense-faculties, self, and consciousness.
Since the apprehended object does not exist,
the fundamental consciousness that acts as the subject of cognition likewise arises [in its absence].
If one relies on the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, then habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and so forth are not the objects of this consciousness.
If one relies on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, however...
According to this treatise, the auditory object and the seven types of consciousness, etc.,
are not its objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
The manifest sense faculties, consciousnesses,
and so forth are likewise not the objective realms manifested by this consciousness.
How can such contradictions be reconciled?
Answer: This is not contradictory.
Why? Because it is not by means of speech that one takes only such phenomena as an object.
This is not because other dharmas are not their objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
Question: Although there is no contradiction, there is nevertheless a difference.
"May I hear the meaning of these differences?
The answer to the meaning of these differences:
Each has its own rationale,
as in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*,
which seeks to clarify the manifestation of all phenomena.
All these are manifestations of the fundamental consciousness;
apart from consciousness,
there are no other phenomena whatsoever.
Therefore, it is taught that there are only the manifest phenomena and the habitual tendencies as seeds.
Its characteristics are not manifest and are no different from consciousness;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises,
in order to demonstrate that no characteristic exists apart from one's own mental continuum as perceived by the mind,
the mind and mental factors are excluded.
All other phenomena within the various continuums,
as well as all mental phenomena, are said to be that which is cognized by this consciousness.
Since it cannot be established apart from the dust and its meaning is self-evident,
it is not explained separately.
The intent behind the disappearance [of the teachings] as revealed in other treatises may be understood by analogy with this;
one must not adhere dogmatically to a single perspective.
This is because it slanders a comprehensive teaching.
Let us now cease this digression and explain the main text.
Regarding the fourth, "wisdom-consciousness" (*jñāna-vijñāna*): this is the first of the six aspects [of the seventh consciousness], namely, the aspect of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
The fruits of craving are termed defiled and pure phenomena;
one discriminates those phenomena because of the reckoning of "I" and "mine."
This refers to the discrimination of defiled and pure phenomena.
"Continuing consciousness" is precisely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
it is the characteristic of continuity among the six aforementioned characteristics.
"Because it is not severed through association with mindfulness" refers to the non-interruption of its own essence;
this explains the meaning of the term "continuity.
From "maintaining" onwards...
Explaining the term "continuity" by way of its functional capacity:
this consciousness is able to give rise to craving and grasping.
It can draw forth and sustain the various formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by past ignorance,
enabling them to become the existence (*bhava*) capable of bringing about future fruits;
therefore, it is said that it maintains and sustains past results so that they are not lost.
This meaning is fully explained as set forth in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Furthermore, consciousness is able to give rise to the afflictions that moisten rebirth,
and it can cause the continuity of karmic results to proceed without interruption.
Therefore, it is said that they accomplish the retributions of the present and future without discrepancy.
Thus, the causal flow of the three periods of time proceeds without interruption;
because its function lies in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*).

The statement, "Reflecting on what has already passed and contemplating what lies in the future," demonstrates that the function of this consciousness differs from that of the *jñāna-vijñāna* (cognitive wisdom),
because the latter only takes present objects as its domain.
This is proven by this textual passage.
Therefore, it is known that this continuous consciousness is precisely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This is not the same as the aforementioned explanation of the continuous mind (*saṃtānacitta*).
Therefore, from here on, [the text] establishes the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The five kinds of consciousness and so forth explained above have no separate self-nature,
for they all depend upon the principle of the one mind.
The three realms are false and illusory;
they are produced solely by the mind.

It is said that all phenomena arise from deluded thoughts, and all discrimination is but the discrimination of one’s own mind. When the mind does not see the mind, there are no characteristics to be apprehended. As a verse in the ten-fascicle sutra says:
If the body, the means of subsistence,
and the environment were like what is seen in a dream,
there would have to be two kinds of mind within that experience.
Yet they lack the characteristic of duality;
just as a blade cannot cut itself,
nor can a finger point to itself.
Just as the eye cannot see itself,
so too is this matter.
What is the meaning of this?
If the various things seen in a dream were real in the manner they appear,
then there would be duality.
Yet within that dream, there is in reality no duality of the apprehending subject and the apprehended object;
all minds of the three realms are just like this dream.
Therefore, it is said that all conceptualization is the conceptualization of one's own mind;
yet this mind cannot see itself, just as a sword blade or a finger cannot point to themselves.
Therefore it is said that the mind does not see the mind;
in its manifestation, there is nothing else to be seen,
nor does it see itself.
Then there is nothing seen.
Because that which is seen does not exist,
the seeing itself cannot be established.
The seer and the seen are both unattainable;
apart from these, there is nothing else.
Furthermore, what characteristics [would there be]?
Therefore, it is said that no characteristic can be apprehended. As that verse says:
It is neither other nor caused;
it is not a conceptualization of conceptualized objects.
It consists of the five dharmas and the two minds.
In the state of tranquility, there is nothing such as this.
Question: As stated in various treatises such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, both the mind and mental factors all realize their own intrinsic natures (*svasaṃvedana*).
This is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it were otherwise,
it would be like something never before seen.
One should not dwell upon such thoughts.
Regarding this, the sutra states:
"One does not see it in this way."
How are these contradictions to be reconciled?
The answer is: there is a different intention here;
it is intended that they not be contradictory.
What is meant?
The intention of this sutra and treatise is to clarify that apart from the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part), there is no separate *nimitta-bhāga* (objectified part).
The image-part (nimittabhāga) appears as having nothing seen;
nor can it be said that this very seeing-part (darśanabhāga) turns back to see the seeing-part itself,
because these two do not function reciprocally and because they arise directed outwardly.
Therefore, a finger pointing at itself is used as an analogy for the same principle.
According to the intent of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*,
although its seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) cannot see itself, [it can still perceive objects].
However, there exists the function of the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga),
which is able to verify the substance of the seeing portion (darśanabhāga);
this is because their functions are distinct.
Because it arises directed inwardly,
the flame of a lamp is used as a homologous example (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*). For this reason:
They are not contradictory.
Furthermore, within this sutra and its treatise,
it is for the purpose of revealing the true nature (dharmatā).
Regarding the meaning of non-existence,
the author of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states that there is no intrinsic view.
Because provisional designations are established,
it is said that there is self-cognition based on what is not non-existent in meaning.
However, conventional designations do not move within the true mark,
and the true mark does not harbor conventional designations;
because it does not harbor them, it does not move.
What contradiction is there?
It is as stated here:
because there is no characteristic apart from seeing.
It is the characteristic of seeing versus non-seeing.
However, since other passages state that the *nimittabhāga* (objective part) is not the *darśanabhāga* (subjective part), it follows that the *darśanabhāga* is able to see the *nimittabhāga*.
Why should such contradictions not be considered strange?
One should know that,
as before, they do not harbor mutual resentment.
Furthermore, it is said:
in order to manifest that [the object] exists as a conceptual designation (prajñapti-sat), it is stated that it possesses both aspect (ākāra) and seeing (darśana).
To reveal that the conventional is non-existent,
it is said to be "without marks" and "without seeing.
Because conventional existence is not to be regarded as truly existent, [it is so described].
One does not waver in non-existence,
for since provisional non-existence does not correspond to ultimate non-existence;
nor does one harbor attachment to existence.
Because they do not harbor [the notion] of existence,
they appear as if existing; because they do not move toward non-existence, they are quiescent.
Yet it is as if it were not there;
thus, this profoundly deep principle of dependent origination is desolate and without basis.
It is vast and unobstructed;
how could one possibly harbor dissent or dispute within it?
Furthermore, from the passage below:
The second section explains the gateway of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The mental consciousness is still the same as the preceding continuous consciousness;
however, it is designated as such from the perspective of its capacity to arise in conjunction with coarse thoughts of dharma-clinging (*dharmagrāha*) that occur subsequently.
It is called the "continuously succeeding consciousness" (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).
This is designated from the perspective of its arising from preceding moments and its capacity to give rise to the afflictions of views and craving.
It is called "mental consciousness.
Therefore, when one speaks of "mental consciousness," it refers precisely to this continuous consciousness.

The sixth superior characteristic, the characteristic of internal feeling, is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). These characteristics are subsumed within this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
furthermore, this treatise proceeds for now by way of the single gate of mental consciousness.
The characteristics of the five consciousnesses are not presented separately;
the meaning of the text can be understood from this.
As for the passage beginning with "based on the perfuming of ignorance," and so forth:
The second section further elucidates the essence and characteristics of causes and conditions;
herein there are two parts.
The first concerns the essence of the mind.
This reveals that the essence and characteristics of the cause are difficult to fathom in terms of defilement and purity.
The section beginning with "Second, failing to comprehend" below discusses various aspects of defilement and purity.
Regarding the first section, "Clarifying the Meaning of the Distinctions in the Substance and Characteristics of Conditions," the initial statement,

"consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance," reiterates what was previously explained regarding the existence of ignorance based on the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which arises through non-awakening.
This passage precisely clarifies that the intrinsically pure mind (prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta) is moved by the wind of ignorance;
therefore, it is said to be "consciousness arising from ignorance.
As for the essence of this mind:
If it were simply that the mind is perpetually arising and ceasing and is inherently defiled,
then it would not be difficult to understand.
Furthermore, if it were eternally abiding and solely pure mind,
it would likewise not be difficult to know.
Even if its essence were truly pure,
it could still be easily understood as being similar to that which is defiled.
If the substance of consciousness is mobile while its empty nature is quiescent,
what difficulty is there in understanding this?
Now, this mind is pure in essence yet defiled in essence;
it is active in its movement yet still in its nature.
Defilement and purity are non-dual; movement and stillness are not distinct.
Being neither dual nor distinct, they are yet not one.
Because it is thus severed, it is difficult to know.
To say that the self-nature of the mind is pure yet possesses a defiled mind clarifies that while it is pure, it is perpetually defiled.
That although there is a defiled mind, it never turns back from its constant state clarifies that while it moves, it is eternally still.
For this reason, only the Buddha has thoroughly realized it,
as stated in the Ten-Scroll Sūtra:
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is by nature pure,
while adventitious afflictions defile it and render it impure;
it is based on this meaning that I [teach].
For the sake of Queen Śrīmālā and other bodhisattvas,
he taught that the tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna arise together with the seven consciousnesses; this is called the characteristic of transformation and cessation.
O Mahāmati, the realm of the Tathāgatagarbha-Ālayavijñāna—
I now [reveal it] to you and to all the bodhisattvas who possess profound wisdom.
One who is able to discern and differentiate these two kinds of dharmas cannot be understood by other śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths who are attached to mere names;
they are unable to comprehend such two dharmas.
This refers precisely to that.
From "Not attaining" (*buddha*) onwards,
it clarifies the essence, characteristics, and the meaning of the distinctions of conditions.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, the clarification of the distinctions among the various defiled characteristics, their coarse manifestations, and the stages and levels for their remedial abandonment.
Second, the meaning of "concomitance" (saṃprayoga), from the phrase "as follows" onwards.
This clarifies the meaning of the association and non-association of various defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭa-dharma*).
Furthermore, from the section "Moreover, the meaning of the defiled mind" onwards,
it cites various defiled phenomena to clarify the meaning of the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).
The beginning and middle also consist of three parts:
first, the characteristics of ignorance are clarified;
second, the distinctions of the defiled mind are clarified.
This also reveals that the subsequent section clarifies the cultivation and abandonment,
whereas the preceding section does not clarify cultivation and abandonment.
The reason they are not presented in sequential order is that [the author] intends to clarify the manner of gradually treating ignorance directly,
rather than merely demonstrating the removal of deeply defiled states of mind.
From the coarse to the subtle,
this enables the fundamental ignorance to be gradually abandoned and progressively relinquished according to its presence.
For this reason, the exposition of the cessation [of defilements] is not treated here,
but will be explained later.
In this context, what is referred to as "defiled" is the aforementioned mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
together with the opening of the five types of mind.
However, because the process of elimination proceeds from the coarse to the subtle, they are explained in reverse order.

First, regarding the defilement associated with attachment: this refers to the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation that arise from the aforementioned mental consciousness.
As stated above:
reckoning "self" and "what belongs to self," there are various kinds of false attachments.
Up to this point, because it is the basis for consciousness and has the sense of increasing the afflictions of views and craving,

it is said that "the stage associated with faith" (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) is able to abandon them; this refers to the stage of the Ten Understandings (*daśa-avabodha*) within the Three Degrees of Worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇaka*).
As stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*:
"The noble embryo of the patience of submission consists of thirty stages: the ten faiths, the ten minds, and the mind of the worthy."
Upon entering this stage,
the coarse afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation can no longer manifest.
Therefore, it is called "detachment.
One should know that this is what is clarified throughout the preceding and following sections of this treatise.
All of these explain the antidotes and abandonment in terms of active manifestation (*samudācāra*),
without considering the seeds (*bīja*).
Therefore, there is also a "suspended bead" regarding the stages and grounds for the treatment and abandonment as explained in other sūtras;
this should not be considered strange.
Regarding the second type, the defilement associated with non-interruption: among the five kinds of mind, it is the fifth, the *prabandha-vijñāna* (continuity-consciousness).

Because it is associated with the grasping at a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*) and is uninterrupted, when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-darśana*) upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), [it is severed].
This is ultimate detachment.
Regarding the third, the defilement associated with discerning cognition (*viniścaya-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), it corresponds to the fourth consciousness among the five mental states.
From the seventh stage downward,
when the two types of emptiness arise,
they no longer manifest as active functions.
When emerging from contemplation and dwelling in the state of a mind that functions spontaneously in accordance with the conventional world,
these [defilements] may also manifest.
Therefore, it is said that they gradually depart;
from the seventh stage onward,
they are forever extinguished and do not arise again.
This is called "ultimate detachment.
This meaning is as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Regarding its seeds:
It is only upon reaching the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) that they are suddenly severed,
as is explained in detail within the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*.
The three preceding defilements have coarse modes of activity and possess the three types of equality.
Therefore, it is called "associated.

Regarding the fourth, the defilement of the non-associated manifesting-form: this refers to the third consciousness among the five mental consciousnesses, the manifesting-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), because it manifests all forms and images like a clear mirror.
The stage of mastery over form is the eighth bhūmi.

Regarding the fifth [point], "being able to see the defilements dissociated from mind": among the five [consciousnesses], it refers to the second, the evolving consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna), because it is able to perceive signs based upon the moving mind.
The Stage of Mastery over the Mind is the ninth stage.

Regarding the defilements that are not associated with the six fundamental karmas: among the five [consciousnesses], it is the first, the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), which, by the power of ignorance, moves through non-awakened recollection.
The Bodhisattva who has exhausted the stages refers to the tenth stage and the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*);
these are collectively considered a single stage from the perspective of ultimate reality.
The treatise states:
"From the eighth stage upward,
there also arise subtle manifestations."
However, within this stage,
having already attained mastery over the pure land,
coarse form never again manifests.
Therefore, it is said that [the eye] is detached from the ear.
Furthermore, from the ninth bhūmi upward,
there is also a subtle capacity for seeing.
However, because one attains mastery over the mind and perceives that the signs become increasingly subtle,
it is said that they are "detached."
This is how it is known;
therefore, the subsequent text states:
"It relies upon the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*)."
That which is perceived up to the ultimate stage of the Bodhisattva is called the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya).
If one is free from the karmic consciousness (karmavijñāna), [this is so].
Thus, there is no sign of seeing;
yet one knows that as long as the karmic consciousness has not been exhausted,
the faculty capable of seeing does not depart from its characteristic of seeing.
Next, the second section clarifies the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*) and non-association (*asaṃprayoga*).
Of the first three [categories], those that are defiled are termed "associated."
The last three defilements and ignorance are dissociated from the mind;
as stated above, when a thought suddenly arises that is dissociated from the mind, it is called ignorance.
Regarding the diversity of mental factors associated with the mind: this refers to the various dharmas categorized as afflictions (*kleśa*), whose characteristics are each distinct.

This is like the diversity of activities—such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to self (*ātma-sneha*), and the conceit of self (*ātma-māna*)—within the "defilement associated with the discerning cognition" (*vikalpa-jñāna-samprayukta-kleśa*).
The Kātyāyanasūtra states:
"One should know that these are the mind and the mental factors (citta-caitta) which attend to phenomena."
Regarding the phrase "the dharmas that the mind contemplates" herein:
these are the dharmas contemplated by the mind;
they are all alternative names for the mental factors (caitta).

Regarding the distinction between defilement and purity: it refers to the conceptualization of various phenomena as either defiled or pure, such as the discrimination of a self and what belongs to a self.
Regarding the knowledge of similarity: it is the ability to know that things are similar.
Regarding "having the same object-condition" (ālambana-samprayukta):
it means having the same objective referent (ālambana). Herein, the term "associated" (samprayukta) is used based on these three [factors].
To say that the mental factors (caitasika-dharma) are distinct means they share the same essence (tattva).
Among the various afflictions (kleśa),
each has its own single essence.
Because there is no second [nature] in either case:
"the sameness of the object" means the equality of wisdom;
"the sameness of the objective condition" means the equality of the objective support.
Possessing these three meanings, it is called "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*).
Question: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
All minds and mental factors have the same object of cognition (ālambana),
yet they do not possess the same mode of activity (ākāra); they arise simultaneously, each functioning individually.
In this context, the explanation regarding the characteristic of cognition is likewise the same.
How, then, are these contradictions to be reconciled?
The answer is that both meanings are present.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Why? Because, for example, my seeing is the functioning of the nature of seeing.
My love is the nature and practice of love;
such are its distinctions,
each having a different mode of operation.
Furthermore, seeing that craving and the other [afflictions] all act as conditions for a self—
from this perspective of meaning— [it is said].
Because their names and characteristics are known to be identical, we know that these two do not obstruct one another.
The statement that "the mind itself is non-awakened and is eternally without distinction" clarifies the meaning of being without substance and so forth.
Because there are no distinct dharmas categorized as afflictions apart from the mind,
it is said that the mind itself is non-awakened and is always without distinction.
Since its substance and other attributes do not exist, upon what could the remaining two [characteristics] depend?
Therefore, there is no case of simultaneous cognition and simultaneous object-conditioning;
hence it is said that they do not mutually condition one another through simultaneous cognition.
Question: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The ālayavijñāna is associated with the five [mental factors];
this is the defiled mind capable of seeing within it.
Why is it said here that they are dissociated?
The answer is: the intention of this treatise is to proceed according to the distinctions in the enumeration of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is called association (*samprayoga*).
It is able to perceive the defilement of the mind,
yet it does not belong to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*).
They are called "non-associated," and thus there is no contradiction;
although there are five subtle universal factors in number.
The mind penetrates phenomena as being signless,
yet because it grasps at signs,
this is an attachment to phenomena.
Since there is no separate perception of a numerical enumeration of dharmas,
there is no separate grasping at the selfhood of phenomena (dharma-ātman).
This is how it is known.
The ālayavijñāna is also characterized by the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*,
this occurs from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
All afflictions no longer manifest; there remains only the cognitive obscuration.
Because it serves as the basis,
within this state, the afflictions of the other seven consciousnesses [are suppressed].
None of these manifest;
only the ālayavijñāna manifests. Therefore, it is known.
This consciousness is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
If one discusses that which possesses seeds, these are the seeds of the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Since it is likewise not yet exhausted,
we know that his statement refers specifically to the active (manifest) cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "defiled mind" (kliṣṭa-citta) and below:
this third section establishes the two obstacles (āvaraṇa).
Now, as for the meaning of these two obstacles:
Briefly, there are two gates;
each pair abandons the pervasive obstacles and the ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).
That which causes one to wander in saṃsāra and obstructs the fruit of nirvāṇa is called the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa).
The specific obstacles for Bodhisattvas are the afflictions such as attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
which cause delusion regarding the objects of knowledge and obstruct the fruit of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
This is called the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This section is as described in other sūtras and treatises.
Second, all minds that involve movement of thought and grasping at signs.
That which contravenes the tranquil nature of the wisdom of suchness is called the hindrance of afflictions;
it is fundamental ignorance.
To be in a state of unconscious stupor,
thereby contravening the function of discernment of wisdom that accords with reality,
is termed "obstruction of wisdom."
In this treatise, with reference to the meaning of the latter category,
six types of defiled minds are taught.
The obstacle of afflictions is called the ground where ignorance dwells;
the obstacle to knowledge is called the obstacle of wisdom.
Nevertheless, since they correspond [to one another],
ignorance should obstruct intuitive wisdom (*jñāna*),
and the defiled mind should obstruct valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Why is this not so? Because it is not necessarily so.
The sense of "not necessarily" is as explained in the treatise itself.
Section Five:
Furthermore, from "below this" onwards,
the characteristics of arising and ceasing are explained in detail, as established in the preceding section on the Establishment of the Thesis.
Within this, there are two parts.
The first clarifies the coarse and subtle characteristics of arising and ceasing.
The following section [consists of] these two.
Next, the meaning of the cessation of the coarse and the subtle is explained.
This section also has two parts:
first, the actual explanation of the coarse and the subtle; second, their differentiation according to persons.

Regarding the statement that "the characteristics of arising and ceasing are of two kinds," this clarifies that the phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of arising and ceasing possess both coarse and subtle aspects;
it does not mean that within each moment of arising and ceasing there exists a gross entity and a minute one.
First, those that are coarse and associated with the mind: among the six kinds of defilements, the first three are associated with the mind;
because their characteristics are coarse and manifest, they are called "characteristic arising and ceasing."
Second, as for those that are subtle and dissociated from the mind: the latter three defilements are dissociated;
they lack the characteristics of coarse mental factors and their distinctions.
Its substance is subtle and minute,
flowing constantly without interruption;
therefore, it is called "continuous arising and ceasing."
As it says in the ten-fascicle sutra:
"There are two kinds of cessation of consciousness. What are these two?"
First is cessation by characteristic;
second is cessation by continuity.
The same applies to arising and abiding.
The *Catur-varga-sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of consciousness:
that which is described as the flow of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and that which is the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the marks [of phenomena]."
It is also like this:
in the sūtras, only two names are directly mentioned,
without separately manifesting their specific characteristics.
Therefore, in this treatise, the author clarifies their characteristics by distinguishing them in relation to persons:
among the coarse [levels], the first two of the three are the coarsest;
among the subtle [levels], the first two of the three are the coarsest.
The subtle within the coarse consists of the first of each of the three periods (beginning, middle, and end).
The subtle within the subtle consists of the last of each of the three periods.
These correspond to the first two of the middle three periods.
Both are present in the mental consciousness;
their modes of activity are coarse,
and they are known by ordinary persons.
The first, middle, and last [moments] are one;
this is the seventh consciousness,
whose mode of activity is not coarse.
That which is not realized by ordinary beings refers to the first two among the middle [three];
these distinguish the subject and object as known by Bodhisattvas.
The final one is—
The distinction between the perceived and the perceiving has not yet been made; only a Buddha thoroughly understands this.
The following clarifies the meaning of cessation.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning of cessation:
first, the conditions for wisdom are clarified.
To state that the two kinds of arising and ceasing exist based on the permeation of ignorance is a general statement.
The following section specifically clarifies the causes and conditions.
What is called "the meaning of non-awakening" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
"Falsely creating objects" refers to the objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).
Speaking generally,
both types of arising and ceasing take ignorance as their cause and objective conditions as their缘 (pratyaya). However, when discussed specifically:
Due to the cause of ignorance,
a non-associated mind arises;
due to the condition of the object-field.
It arises in association with the mind;
now, regarding the time of its cessation,
it is explained for the sake of a specific perspective.
It is said that because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases; because the object-condition ceases, the associated mind ceases.
To explain according to their full meaning, each of these two types has two further divisions.
As stated in the four-fascicle *Sūtra*:
"O Mahāmati, there are inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation."
This is the cause of the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Grasping at various objects and the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false discrimination are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*nirūpaṇa-vastu-vijñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "inconceivable permeation," it means that ignorance is able to permeate the *tathatā* (suchness) because it is immeasurable.
The inconceivable reversal refers to that which cannot be [achieved] through the perfuming of the love for True Suchness or by ignorance.
It pervades and then returns;
therefore, this perfuming and its reversal are extremely subtle and hidden.
Therefore, the mode of appearance of the manifest consciousness that arises is subtle and not associated [with mental factors].
As for the phrase "beginningless delusive appearances":
This very manifest consciousness,
because it has never been separated from conceptualization since time immemorial,
is as stated in the preceding passage:
Since beginningless time,
it has never been separated from thought;
therefore, it is called "beginningless ignorance."
The meaning of beginningless false conceptualization is also like this.
As for what is called "various objects":
It is like the various objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
By means of these two factors, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *ālayavijñāna* are perfumed and stirred, causing the waves of the seven consciousnesses to arise;
this is because both false discrimination and its objects are coarse and manifest.
The seven consciousnesses that arise constitute the associated mind (*samprayukta-citta*).
Now, within this treatise:
Because it mentions only one side, it is subtle;
therein, it speaks only of the permeation of ignorance. Because it is coarse, [it mentions both].
This refers solely to the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It is explained according to the principle of proceeding from the subtle to the coarse,
in order to clarify the distinct characteristics of the various types of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, in the four-fascicle sutra,
it says: "O Mahāmati,
if that true consciousness is concealed..."
When various unrealities and all false delusions are extinguished,
then all consciousnesses of marks are extinguished;
this is called the extinction of marks.
Regarding the cessation of the continuum:
when the cause of the continuum ceases,
the continuum itself ceases.
When the basis is extinguished and the object is extinguished,
then the continuity is extinguished. Why is this so?
